newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine-Russia Fleet talks end in deadlock - agency.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine-Russia Fleet talks end in deadlock - agency.

text.p: Russian and Ukrainian officials trying to resolve a long-standing row over the Soviet Black Sea Fleet ended talks early on Wednesday with little progress -- and cancelled a planned dinner -- Interfax-Ukraine news agency said.
"A closing session planned for the second half of November 6 did not take place...A joint dinner planned in the preliminary programme did not happen either," the agency said.
Instead, the heads of the two delegations spent 40 minutes talking to Ukrainian Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko and the Russians flew straight home, it said.
The delegations were trying to draw up documents to end years of arguing between the former Soviet neighbours over the fleet, under Russian command but on Ukrainian territory.
Ukrainian government officials were not available for comment.

After years of bickering over where to base the fleet, how Russia should pay to keep it on Ukraine's Crimea peninsula and how it should be divided, the two countries appeared to achieve a breakthrough last month.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin promised Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma when they met in Moscow on October 24 that he would visit Kiev to sign a Friendship Treaty once he had recovered from surgery.
The two men said they had solved all the problems over the dispute. Yeltsin, who had a multiple heart bypass operation on Tuesday, had postponed six trips to Kiev in 20 months.
The delegations on Wednesday were preparing papers for a Cooperation Commission to meet in Kiev later this month, Interfax-Ukraine said.
Delegation members expressed doubt that the documents would be ready for the session on November 15 -- the day Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin is also due to visit Kiev.
Volodymyr Horbulin, Secretary of the Security and Defence Council and Kuchma's closest aide, told reporters earlier that he did not expect Chernomyrdin to make the trip.
"There is no sense in his coming empty-handed. The visit should be properly prepared," Horbulin said.
He also said, without giving details, that the Russians had changed their position slightly.
But whatever Kuchma and Yeltsin might agree, they are unlikely to please nationalist sentiment at home.
Moscow mayor Yuri Luzhkov -- a potential successor to Yeltsin -- argues that Ukraine has no legal title to Sevastopol, headquarters of the Black Sea fleet.

Last week, he described the city as "literally drenched in the blood of Russians", a reference to its fate as a battleground in the 19th century Crimean War against Turkey, Britain and France and against Germany in World War Two.
The mayor of the Ukrainian Black Sea port of Odessa responded angrily to Luzhkov's comments in an article in the Russian daily Izvestia on Wednesday.

"If we start trying to work out where the Russians, the Ukrainians -- or the Germans or the Chinese and so on -- built towns and then shed blood, that is a direct route either to the madhouse or to World War Three," he wrote.
